title: Loop Control: break & continue 🎮
description: Take full command of loops – skip iterations, bail out early, and tame nested beasts.

slides.title: Taking Control 🕹️
slides.content:
## Beyond the Condition

Sometimes you need to:
- Exit a loop immediately when a certain event occurs.
- Skip the rest of the current iteration and move to the next.

Bash provides:
- `break` – exit the loop entirely.
- `continue` – jump to the next iteration.

slides.title: break Example
slides.content: Search for a number and stop:
slides.codeSnippet:
for i in {1..10}; do
  if [ $i -eq 5 ]; then
    echo "Found 5, stopping."
    break
  fi
  echo "Checking $i"
done

quizData.question: What does `break` do inside a loop?

options.text: Restarts the loop from the beginning

quizData.explanation: `break` exits the loop entirely, no matter the condition.

slides.title: continue Example
slides.codeSnippet:
for (( i=1; i<=10; i++ )); do
  if (( i % 2 == 0 )); then
    continue
  fi
  echo "$i"
done

quizData.question: Which keyword skips the rest of the current loop iteration and proceeds with the next?
quizData.explanation: `continue` stops executing the current iteration and moves to the next evaluation of the loop condition.

slides.title: Nested Loops & `break n` 🪆
slides.content:
## Break Out of Multiple Levels

When loops are nested, `break` by default exits only the innermost loop. Use `break n` to break out of `n` enclosing loops.

```bash
for i in {1..3}; do
   for j in {1..3}; do
      if [ $j -eq 2 ]; then
         break 2  # exits both loops
      fi
   done
done
```
`continue n` works similarly for skipping outer iterations.

slides.title: break 2 Demo
slides.codeSnippet:
for x in A B C; do
  for y in 1 2 3; do
    if [ "$x$y" = "B2" ]; then
      echo "Breaking at B2"
      break 2
    fi
    echo "$x$y"
  done
done
echo "Done"

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Break out of a `while` or `until` loop with `break` just as you do with `for`. The same rules apply.
